The First Conditional in Negative
We use the first conditional to talk about a possible condition and its outcome in the future.

The first conditional has two clauses, the first clause (condition) with 'if' in present simple and the second clause (result) with the tense in future simple. In this case, we are going to study the negative form. Let’s see the structures:

Quantifiers
A quantifier is a word or phrase that indicates the amount or number we want to give to someone or something.

Quantifiers can be used with both, count nouns and non-count nouns. Today, we are going to study too much and too many. 

Too much is used with non-count nouns. Let’s see the next example:

There is too much information about programming paradigms.

 As you can see, you always use there is with the quantifier too much.

 Too many is used with count nouns. Let’s see the next example:

 There are too many paradigms involved in the execution model of a language.

 As you can see, you always use there are with the quantifier too many.

images.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen! Today, we will talk about software paradigms, also known as programming paradigms, and their different types. If you don't understand what I'm saying, please stop me, and I'll clarify any doubts. Let's begin! As you know, there is too much information about programming paradigms, but first, we are going to start with the basics. We use programming paradigms as a method to classify programming languages which are categorized by the style of the computer programming. In other words, if a language doesn't have particular traits, you can't determine what programming paradigm it belongs to. There are too many paradigms that focus on the language's execution model. However, there are others that are more concerned about how the code is organized by groups.

Among the most common programming paradigms are imperative paradigm, which allows side effects; declarative paradigm, which doesn't state the order of the executed operations; functional paradigm, which excludes the side effects. Additionally, we have object-oriented paradigm, which organizes groups of codes; different from procedural paradigm, which organizes codes into functions. We also have logic paradigm, which needs a certain execution model. Finally, we have symbolic paradigm, which has a particular style of grammar and syntax. I know there is too much to learn; however, I'm going to give you a few examples later.

Languages that are part of imperative paradigm have two important characteristics: the first one is that it allows side effects and also guides the order of the operations with constructs that command that order; and the second one consists of controlling the flow in an explicit sequence of commands. Meanwhile, declarative paradigm states the result of the executed operations, but it doesn't state the order of the process itself. In other words, if you don't want to know the conditions of the number of operations that can be used, you will use declarative paradigm. In object-oriented paradigm, you build the codes as objects, which you can change for the same code in the same object. </br>
Well, I think that's all for today. Remember, there are too many programming paradigms, review them all the time.  If you don't research more about these concepts, you won't learn how to classify programming languages easily!
